data.title: Anthropic researcher claims to solve Riemann maths problem with Claude
data.description:
ON THE heels of Anthropic PBC’s record-breaking initial public offering, a researcher at the company said he believes he used its artificial intelligence software to solve a famous number theory problem that has plagued mathematicians for more than 150 years.

Mathematician Levent Alpoge published a note on his personal website on Friday (Nov 20), claiming to have come up with a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. He shared a link to code written in the programming language Lean that he said showed evidence of his success. 

According to his note, Alpoge messaged Anthropic chief executive officer Dario Amodei on Sunday night to ask about announcing his findings to the public.

Alpoge called the timing of his announcement “horrible,” but said, “I just could not live if I waited even longer.” Anthropic declined to comment, and Alpoge did not respond to a request to comment.

The Riemann hypothesis relates to the distribution of prime numbers and has long been considered one of the most difficult math problems in the field.

OpenAI and Anthropic have been working for years to demonstrate the advanced capabilities of their most cutting-edge models by solving challenging math and life sciences problems. 

If confirmed, Alpoge’s work would mark the second Millennium Prize Problem that may have been solved by AI; OpenAI said its models had generated a solution to the 90-year-old Navier-Stokes problem in September. 

Andrew Sutherland, a senior research scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said he verified Alpoge’s work about the Riemann hypothesis on his computer and has seen at least three other verifications on multiple systems from other professional mathematicians.

Alpöge’s efforts with Claude build on the work of many mathematicians who have studied the Riemann hypothesis, as well as the field of mathematic formalisation, according to Sutherland.

“I am both very nervous and very excited” for the future, Sutherland said, explaining that mathematicians have years ahead to dig into this proof to understand how it can be applied. “This is a day for celebration,” Sutherland said, even as he acknowledged the concerns in his field about AI’s potential impacts the math profession and other jobs.

Noah Giansiracusa, an associate professor of math at Bentley University and faculty associate at Harvard University, added that, if the solution works, it’s a big deal for AI.

“It sounds like there’s a pretty good chance this is airtight and valid,” Giansiracusa said.

Alpoge described the experience of attempting to prove the problem as a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt.” 

“Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpoge wrote. BLOOMBERG

data.title: AI can manage a familyâs wealth. It cannot decide what the wealth is for
data.description:
WITHIN a few years, artificial intelligence will take over much of the work in managing family wealth.

Consolidating accounts across entities, checking documents against the law, drafting and monitoring agreements, producing reports on every holding – tasks that occupy accountants, lawyers and family office staff are being automated.

Singapore and Hong Kong, where governments have actively courted family offices, will be among the first places to feel the change.

Consider a typical family that owns three operating companies and a portfolio managed by its single family office in Singapore.

A reporting system pulls figures from all of them every morning. Each company is ahead of budget, and the portfolio is performing better than its benchmark. By every measure on the screen, the year is a success.

Yet, the family has agreed that it will buy out two cousins and that the founder may start a new venture. Neither is communicated to the system; nothing says that the next three years must produce cash to fund these decisions.

Each company owned by the family reinvests its profits, as a well-run company should, and the system reports that this is going well because it was not made aware of new requirements.

The family office uses an investment platform that rebalances the portfolio towards its benchmark. The model finds regional property underweight and adds to it. The family’s largest company is a property developer.

Seen from the portfolio’s perspective, the allocation is balanced. Seen from that of the family, its exposure to one market has just gone up disproportionately.

Then a tax tool optimises the group’s structure. It works from the companies’ figures and assumes, as the companies do, that profits are reinvested. Corporate tax falls.

It does not consider tax on dividends because nothing the tool was given says the owners intend to withdraw cash. The plan is optimal for the companies; it is expensive for the family members when they are hit by their tax bill for taking out cash for the buyout and new venture.

Each answer provided by the system is correct. Each system optimises what it was given: the companies’ budgets, the portfolio’s benchmark, the companies’ tax. Each receives its instructions through a different channel.

None of them knows what the owners need, and the whole infrastructure drifts away from the family’s goals.

Compliance, relational, perspective

One way to see where this gap lies is through what I call “the three functions of ownership”: compliance, relational and perspective.

Compliance ensures all aspects of ownership, such as tax and regulatory rules, abide by the law. The law is codified, so much of this task will be automated by AI.

Relational is what the owners agree among themselves: the direction for their wealth, its limits, who acts on their behalf and what is reported back to them. Drafting and monitoring such agreements will also be largely automated, but the agreement itself remains a decision only the owners can take.

Perspective carries the agreement through. It gives each significant investment and business holding a mandate, assesses the strategy proposed to meet it, takes important decisions back to the family and tracks the results.

It does so with the family’s whole wealth in view, optimising within the limits that compliance sets, and, most importantly, reaches the organisation through one channel: the person leading the wealth on the owners’ behalf.

In the hypothetical family above, the chain breaks between the relational and perspective functions.

The owners have an agreement, but it was not decided and written down in the language of perspective. There is nothing to carry through, so each system optimises against the goals of a company or a portfolio instead.

Decisions still rest with the family

Today, an experienced finance director or family office head who knows what the owners want might catch all three concerns: question the reinvestment plans, notice the added property exposure, ask about dividend tax.

AI can do the same analysis, faster and across every holding, but only if the owners’ requirements have been established. Without that, automation does not close the gap. It makes the gap more consequential.

Closing the chain starts with a clearly communicated agreement. The family decides that they need cash over the next three years for the buy out and the venture, that their investment portfolio should factor in their property company, and that their taxes should be optimised for taking money out.

The person leading the wealth then turns that into instructions every system can work from.

Each company gets a mandate for what it must pay out, so its budget includes the cash the owners need.

The investment platform gets a limit on property allocation for the whole wealth, so owning a property developer does not unbalance the portfolio.

The tax tool is told that cash will be paid out, so dividend tax is part of the plan.

With that in place, AI can do what it does best. It flags the conflicts before the budgets are approved, before the platform rebalances and before the tax plan is adopted. The owners’ time is then spent on the decisions that are theirs.

For advisers, the shift is just as large. Much of what is billed today in compliance and relational work will be done by machines. The value that remains lies in helping owners define what the AI should serve.

AI will make it ever easier to produce information, assess alternatives and carry out decisions. None of that establishes what the wealth is supposed to bring the family. That remains with them, and carrying it through requires a function of its own.

The writer is founder of H S Nielsen, which advises owners of complex wealth structures

The commentary is based on the writer’s own experiences, observations and argument. AI tools were used for drafting in English and editing. The writer remains fully accountable for the commentary’s accuracy, originality and final form.

data.title: Chinaâs offshore tax clampdown pushes budget into rare surplus
data.description:
CHINA’S budget swung into a rare surplus in October, as tighter scrutiny of offshore wealth produced a one-off bonanza of individual income tax receipts and offset a long-awaited increase in fiscal spending.

A broad measure of government revenue exceeded expenditure by 265.7 billion yuan (US$39.8 billion) last month, resulting in the first surplus in a year, according to Bloomberg calculations based on data published by the Ministry of Finance on Friday (Nov 20).

Authorities collected more than 296 billion yuan from individual income tax in the month, up nearly 90 per cent from a year earlier.

Beijing has embarked on its most aggressive tax enforcement campaign in decades, tightening oversight of offshore trusts set up by citizens and strengthening compliance. The government has been looking for ways to make up for huge declines in income from land sales, as a housing downturn shows no signs of a turnaround.

“The move against offshore trusts was an unusually fast and significant change in tax rules,” Gavekal Dragonomics analysts led by Christopher Beddor said in a report this week.

“China’s tax officials are using much-improved surveillance capabilities to bring more wealthy households into the tax net, upending long-established tax strategies,” they said. “They have given every indication there will be more enforcement actions to come, bolstered by expanding legal authorities.”

Tax payments on income earned through offshore trusts surged last month as taxpayers rushed to declare and settle outstanding liabilities before a late October deadline to avoid extra charges under rules introduced in July.

More than 120 billion yuan in such payments alone flowed into government coffers last month, the official Xinhua News Agency reported earlier.

The haul helped push up broad fiscal revenue, which rose 1.7 per cent on year in the first 10 months to almost 22.5 trillion yuan. That means 80.6 per cent of this year’s official income target has already been achieved, approaching the goal at the fastest since 2021.

The government also accelerated spending in October after rolling out a modest stimulus package that focused on investment in major national infrastructure projects such as the Six Networks.

Broad expenditure expanded 4.7 per cent last month from a year earlier, its first increase in eight months. The growth helped narrow a drop in total budget spending to 2.9 per cent in the January-October period from a 3.5 per cent decline in the first three quarters of the year.

Still, the expansion in government spending was insufficient to arrest a contraction in investment, leaving the economy more vulnerable. Fixed-asset investment plunged 17 per cent last month from a year earlier, according to estimates by Bloomberg Economics, its sharpest fall outside the Covid pandemic.

The deployment of previously raised funds has slowed, according to Goldman Sachs Group Inc. economists including Lisheng Wang. Outstanding fiscal deposits in October were 1.6 trillion yuan, or 21 per cent higher than year-earlier levels, widening from 958 billion yuan in September, they wrote in a note after the MOF data release. 

“With this year’s growth target nearly secured, we believe some government funds raised in the fourth quarter may be deployed in the first quarter next year to support growth in 2027,” they said. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Anthropic slides 9.1% to shrink IPO gain as AI trade unravels
data.description:
ANTHROPIC PBC shares erased a portion of their first-day jump on Friday (Nov 20), testing investors’ faith after the AI lab delivered the biggest initial public offering in history.

Shares in the company behind the Claude chatbot plunged almost to the IPO price, before paring the loss to close at US$88.30 each, down 9.1 per cent from the end of their debut on Thursday. The trading gives Anthropic a market value of about US$1.6 trillion, ranking it among the 15 biggest publicly traded companies in the world.

The drop came at the same time as the so-called over-allotment option, also known as a greenshoe, was exercised, allowing the underwriting banks to sell additional shares.

The over-allotment lifted the total raised by Anthropic and the co-founders selling shares in the offering to US$119.5 billion, with US$93.5 billion in the IPO and US$26 billion from the concurrent private placement.

“There’s a buyers’ strike for Anthropic as well as the wider AI and tech trade,” according to Emmanuel Valavanis of Forte Securities.

“There are many clients who appear to have been left without allocations and, having been left out of the party, aren’t prepared to pick up the pieces from the hangover. With no skin in the game, and no index considerations for risk of relative performance, investors can sit on the sidelines and wait for longer term price discovery rather than risk getting caught out,” Valavanis said.

Stocks were roiled by a selloff that spread from Asia to the US, with the Nasdaq 100 Index falling 5.6 per cent and the S&P 500 Index sinking 3.7 per cent.

Anthropic’s IPO made history not only because of its size, but also because the company is the first frontier AI model maker to go public. The trading represents a test of whether investors have appetite for companies pioneering the technology itself, rather than the tools to develop it such as chips and data centres. It also sets up a debut for rival OpenAI, which isn’t planning to go public before 2027.

The IPO delivered outsize returns to its backers and pushing up the combined wealth of its seven founders to US$166 billion. The fundraise eclipsed the record set in June by SpaceX’s IPO, which ultimately totaled US$86.2 billion.

Goldman Sachs Group, Morgan Stanley and 20 other banks earned a record US$550 million in fees for their work on Anthropic’s IPO.

“We are impressed by the wealth creation this company is generating, in a matter of a few years and with reasonable free cash flow burn,” said Raphael Thuin, head of capital markets strategies at Tikehau Capital.

“To get exposed to AI though, we tend to favour more diversified businesses, and in any case we would like to see the post IPO volatility fade before engaging further.”

Anthropic won over investors with a focus on enterprise customers, propelling its run-rate revenue — a measure annualised from a shorter period — to US$81 billion as of Oct 31, up US$10 billion from the end of September, its regulatory filings show.

Claude Code, the company’s coding agent for software developers, is widely adopted in the industry and has even been used by Nasa engineers, the filing shows. Anthropic has more than 11,900 customers delivering US$100,000 of revenue each on a trailing 12-month basis as of the end of September, up from about 1,500 in 2025.

Investors considering taking stakes may decide to wait out the market turmoil first. The Cboe Volatility Index, Wall Street’s so-called fear gauge, spiked to more than 29 on Friday morning, well above the level where companies typically consider the market welcoming to IPOs.

“We would look at buying in the open market if the stock get close or even below the IPO price,” said Olivier David, a fund manager at Vega IS.

Anthropic’s listing joins companies linked to AI that have pushed US IPO volume to an all-time high. Including Anthropic, first time stock sales raised US$258 billion this year, beating 2021’s US$195 billion haul, excluding financial vehicles such as blank-cheque firms, data compiled by Bloomberg show. 

“What we saw yesterday was real excitement around a big deal getting done,” said Ann Miletti, head of equity investments at Allspring Global Investments. “That demand is a positive. It doesn’t take away the fear or the worry that we don’t know what we don’t know about AI, and the biggest question in investors’ minds is what are the returns?” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Anthropic CEO vacations at Italian resort after public listing
data.description:
ANTHROPIC PBC chief executive officer Dario Amodei is vacationing at a luxury resort in the south of Italy after completing a blockbuster initial public offering, according to people familiar with the matter.

Amodei’s private jet landed in Brindisi on Italy’s Adriatic coast midday on Friday (Nov 20). Local broadcaster Antenna Sud filmed the tech executive at the airport, and Bloomberg News independently confirmed his arrival.

Amodei is expected to stay for a few days, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss private matters. 

Anthropic declined to comment. 

The Claude chatbot maker had its long-awaited Wall Street debut on Thursday after raising US$107.3 billion in a record-breaking public offering.

Shares of Anthropic soared 17 per cent above their IPO price on the first day of trading but erased most of those gains on Friday, reflecting growing caution about the artificial intelligence trade.

Brindisi is a historic port in Puglia, the region that forms the heel of Italy’s boot. Amodei has previously said he and his wife sometimes visit Italy, where they have a horse. 

“I’ll just look at our horse and I’ll be like, Calypso, who’s our horse, she doesn’t know about any of this,” he previously told Bloomberg’s Emily Chang in an interview on The Circuit. “She’s just a happy horse.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: PM Wong, Li Qiang call for stronger Singapore-China ties amid global uncertainty
data.description:
[BEIJING] With the global environment becoming “more uncertain and complex”, it is important that Singapore and China continue to strengthen the partnership between the two countries, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Saturday (Nov 21), the final day of his four-day visit to China.

This would allow both sides to address common challenges and identify new areas of collaboration, said PM Wong in his opening remarks during his meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang

It was held at the Diaoyutai State Guesthouse in Beijing on Saturday (Nov 21).

This is PM Wong’s second time meeting Li in Beijing since his introductory visit last year at the Premier’s invitation.

Since then, PM noted that Singapore and China has had a “good, constructive discussion” on how to take the cooperation between both countries forward. 

“Both China and Singapore have continued to build on our All-Round High-Quality, Future-oriented Partnership,” he said.

PM Wong also referenced the upcoming Joint Council for Bilateral Cooperation with China, which will be held in the Republic on Sunday.

At the event’s conclusion, he said it is expected to yield more than 20 deliverables spanning areas like trade digitalisation and financial integration.

It will also include research and innovation in the healthcare and education industries.

“That reflects the depth and breadth of our cooperation,” said PM Wong.

The media were allowed to be in attendance only for the first few minutes of the leaders’ meeting

During that time, PM Wong also introduced Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Home Affairs Sim Ann; Minister of State for Manpower and Energy, Trade and Industry Foo Cexiang; and Member of Parliament Hamid Razak.

Premier Li said in Mandarin that by joining hands to foster open development, both China and Singapore can “contribute greater positive energy toward stability and prosperity, both within this region and globally”.

“As a long-standing, friendly neighbour, China is prepared to strengthen strategic communication with Singapore,” said Li.

This includes expanding the partnership toward both countries to produce more tangible outcomes, “all while continuing to enhance the friendship between our two peoples”.

The meeting with Li capped a series of talks for PM Wong with Chinese leaders after he arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Economic Leaders’ Meeting.

On Friday, PM Wong met Chinese President Xi Jinping and spoke of deepening ties between Singapore and China. He also met Beijing party secretary Yin Li, a member of the Communist Party of China’s Political Bureau.

In a social media post after meeting Yin, PM Wong described Beijing as a major research and innovation hub and said “there is much that Singapore and Beijing can do together”.

He said they discussed plans to deepen integration across the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region. These developments, he added, offer “exciting opportunities” for cooperation in areas ranging from technology and innovation to sustainable development and education.

data.title: SoftBankâsÂ Son explored US$1 trillion buyout of SK Hynix: report
data.description:
SOFTBANK Group CEO Masayoshi Son recently approached Wall Street institutions about financing a possible trillion-dollar buyout of South Korea memory chip giant SK Hynix, The Information reported on Friday (Nov 20).

SoftBank and SK Hynix did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment on the report, which cited people familiar with the matter. The Information quoted a SoftBank spokesperson as saying Son was no longer considering such a deal. REUTERS

data.title: Bitcoin falls to more than two-year low as global markets sink
data.description:
BITCOIN fell to the lowest level in over two years, extending its reversal from market darling after the re-election of Donald Trump to a casualty of a broader retreat from speculative bets.

The original cryptocurrency slumped as much as 6.1 per cent to US$57,716, the least since September 2024. It has lost more than half its value since reaching a peak above US$126,000 in October 2025 and is now worth less than it was when crypto-friendly Trump retook the White House. 

Bitcoin has been caught in a confluence of pressures in recent weeks. A hack of Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, at the end of October rattled digital assets, while sweeping Democratic victories in the US midterm elections the following week fuelled concerns that the crypto industry’s push for friendlier rules has lost momentum.

“The broader market has shifted into a sharp lack of confidence, and investors are de-risking,” said Andy Baehr, managing director of asset management at GSR. “Bitcoin is along for the ride here, typically weak in deleveraging environments.”

The latest leg lower has been fuelled by investors pulling money from Bitcoin exchange-traded funds amid an unravelling of the artificial-intelligence trade. Bitcoin ETFs have seen year-to-date outflows of more than US$3 billion. 

The broader backdrop is becoming less favourable as well. For much of the past decade, cryptocurrencies occupied a privileged place in the risk-taking economy. Now a stronger dollar and rising expectations of another Federal Reserve rate increase are adding to the pressure. 

The market is pricing a more aggressive Fed rate hike and slowdown in the AI buildout, prompting “an excessively negative market interpretation right now,” said Fabian Dori, chief investment officer at Sygnum Bank.

On Friday, Bitcoin’s slide triggered the liquidation of roughly US$2 billion in long crypto bets over 24 hours, with Bitcoin positions accounting for the majority of that sum, according to Coinglass data. 

“What made the move so fast was leverage,” said Andrew Yang, research analyst at Kaiko. “As Nasdaq losses deepened again in late-morning New York trading, Bitcoin broke below US$60,000, triggering US$94.6 million in BTC liquidations on Binance, Bybit and OKX in a single hour.”

The downturn is unfolding at what should have been a triumphant moment for the industry. 

With Trump as US president, crypto has secured many of the victories it spent the better part of a decade pursuing: a sympathetic White House, friendlier regulators, institutional acceptance and a legislative framework that increasingly treats digital assets as a permanent part of the financial system.

Yet rather than unleashing a new wave of demand, those milestones have coincided with one of Bitcoin’s deepest retreats in years.

Earlier crypto crashes were punctuated by spectacular failures or waves of forced selling. This downturn has been marked by a steadier erosion in demand. Bitcoin fell even as inflation worries mounted, doing little to bolster its case as a hedge. And when geopolitical turmoil sent investors looking for safety, they turned to traditional havens.

Institutional acceptance hasn’t gone away, but the early enthusiasm has cooled. The question now is whether the biggest buyers will keep adding to their holdings at the pace the industry once expected. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel Infrastructure Trust,  Elite UK Reit, Thakral, Katrina
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 20):

Keppel Infrastructure Trust (KIT) : KIT secured S$200 million in revolving loan facilities, with outstanding loans immediately repayable if its trustee-manager ceases to be wholly owned by Keppel Capital and/or Keppel, or ceases to act as KIT’s trustee-manager and a replacement wholly owned by the Keppel companies is appointed beforehand. Neither trigger had occurred yet, but if either leads to cross defaults, about S$1.9 billion in total facilities could be affected. The counter ended 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Thursday, before the news.

Elite UK Reit : The manager of the real estate investment trust (Reit) submitted a planning application for a 352-bed student accommodation development in Wales. It expects a decision in 2027 and aims to start demolition and construction in 2028, subject to approval. The counter ended 1.7 per cent or £0.005 lower at £0.295 on Thursday, before the news.

Thakral : Thakral is selling its remaining 6.1 per cent stake in The Beauty Tech Group (TBTG), netting S$56.5 million, and expects to record a S$17.9 million gain over its end-June book value of S$38.6 million. Including the partial sale at TBTG’s initial public offering last year, the investment returned about S$70 million in cash to Thakral. The group plans to use the latest proceeds for new investments, its existing businesses and other capital needs. Shares of Thakral ended flat at S$1.45 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Katrina Group : An entity linked to carmaker BYD raised its stake in the F&B operator to 13.09 per cent from 4.91 per cent after buying more than 21 million shares for S$500,000 in an off-market transaction. It became a substantial shareholder in September, when it acquired a 5 per cent stake by buying 12.6 million shares from Katrina’s CEO for S$299,880. Shares of Katrina ended 8.3 per cent or S$0.003 higher at S$0.039 on Thursday, before the news.
